extracted.intended_audience: NeurIPS Datasets & Benchmarks authors, reviewers, and dataset/benchmark research community
extracted.subtask_description: Reflection post from the NeurIPS 2025 Datasets & Benchmarks Track describing the new hosting / metadata / review-process standards that were implemented in 2025 and the empirical outcomes (author and reviewer survey results). The post identifies which paper-quality and dataset-quality criteria worked and which still need development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hosting on persistent public repositories
rubrics_metrics.description: the track introduced rigorous requirements for hosting on persistent public repositories with mandatory Croissant metadata
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Over 80% of accepted papers used a handful of widely adopted platforms: Hugging Face, Kaggle, Dataverse, and OpenML. Another 13% relied on self-hosted or bespoke solutions, with the rest distributed across smaller repositories like Zenodo and the Open Science Framework. The standards aim to 'ensure datasets remain verifiable, accessible, and scientifically impactful over time.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory Croissant machine-readable metadata
rubrics_metrics.description: The majority of accepted papers included required Croissant metadata, though gaps appeared in initial submissions. Missing fields included license information (11.9 percent), dataset descriptions (4.9 percent) and URLs (3.5 percent). Less than one percent failed to include dataset names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Croissant metadata enables automated checklists and standardized dataset summaries within OpenReview. Authors are adapting to structured format requirements; current guidance leaves room for interpretation, particularly regarding licensing documentation and descriptive context in machine-readable form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit dataset license information
rubrics_metrics.description: Where licensing information was provided, authors predominantly selected open and permissive terms, particularly Creative Commons BY 4.0 and CC0 1.0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: License information was one of the most commonly missing metadata fields in initial submissions (11.9% missing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsible AI metadata (provenance, biases, sensitive content)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adoption of the Croissant Responsible AI extension remained minimal. This extension captures data collection practices, biases and sensitive content, but few submissions included RAI-compliant documentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Low adoption of RAI metadata indicates a gap between available standards and practical implementation. Authors need clearer instructions for documenting data provenance, biases, limitations and societal impacts. Platform support for RAI-compliant exports would reduce the documentation burden, and more extensive validation checks at submission time can ensure that the most needed information is provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset accessibility for reviewers (no broken links, manageable size)
rubrics_metrics.description: 77 percent reported that datasets were easy to access. Around 10 percent encountered difficulties, most commonly due to missing or broken links and very large files.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eleven percent did not directly inspect datasets and instead based their evaluations solely on the accompanying papers, suggesting accessibility friction undermines empirical review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for very large datasets (>=1 TB)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common issues involved very large datasets (one terabyte or larger), platform rate limits and occasional instability near submission deadlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Community feedback highlighted clearer self-hosting guidelines and platform partnerships for large datasets as a priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automated metadata reports and compliance checklists
rubrics_metrics.description: 69 percent of reviewers found them useful or very useful, and 70 percent indicated that the compliance checklist helped them assess submissions more efficiently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several reviewers recommended that future iterations of the reports be shorter and more focused. Streamlined automated metadata reports for reviewer efficiency was identified as a development priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset documentation completeness and clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: While most submissions included required fields, gaps in the first submission round revealed a learning curve. Authors are adapting to structured format requirements. Current guidance leaves room for interpretation, particularly regarding licensing documentation and descriptive context in machine-readable form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This could be improved through clearer documentation for metadata submission, and by refining automated validation reporting tools to provide concise, targeted information to authors and reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer expertise matching dataset domain
rubrics_metrics.description: Submissions increasingly span specialized domains including AI for science, medicine, multimodal data and LLM evaluation. The reviewer pool shows limitations in diversity and domain coverage. Each paper requires review by experts in data-centric machine learning as well as domain-specific knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Future iterations would benefit from expanding the reviewer pool to include broader domain expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrated impact: enabling future research
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike algorithmic work with performance metrics, dataset and benchmark impact depends on enabling future research by broadening applicability, surfacing underexplored problems or challenging dominant evaluation paradigms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The track requires shared frameworks to assess data coverage, representativeness and innovation aligned with the community. Next iterations could consider requiring a 'demonstrated impact' section in papers or the review form that map dataset characteristics to evaluation results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real-world impact over methodological novelty alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerns among [authors dissatisfied with review quality] included limited reviewer engagement in rebuttals, reliance on AI-generated feedback and emphasis on methodological novelty over real-world impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 25% of authors indicated review quality needed improvement, citing this overemphasis on novelty as a problem for dataset/benchmark work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standardized requirements aligned with main track
rubrics_metrics.description: paper submission requirements were aligned with the NeurIPS main track, while retaining dataset-specific elements like optional single-blind submission
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These two major changes aim to standardize quality evaluations and transform reproducibility from aspiration to expectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verifiable, accessible, and scientifically impactful datasets over time
rubrics_metrics.description: These standards enabled automated checklists and standardized dataset summaries within OpenReview, streamlining the process to reduce reviewer effort and ensure datasets remain verifiable, accessible, and scientifically impactful over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long-term preservation and verifiability are framed as core obligations for D&B Track datasets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer engagement in rebuttals (not AI-generated)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerns among the latter group included limited reviewer engagement in rebuttals, reliance on AI-generated feedback and emphasis on methodological novelty over real-world impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited as a primary quality issue by the 25% of authors who said review quality needed improvement.
